steps.title: FDI two-digit system (ISO 3950)
steps.body:
First digit = quadrant, second = tooth from the midline.

- Permanent quadrants: **1** upper right, **2** upper left, **3** lower left, **4** lower right.
- Primary quadrants: **5, 6, 7, 8** in the same order.
- Teeth 1–8 permanent (central incisor → third molar), 1–5 primary.

Example: upper right first molar = **16**; lower left primary second molar = **75**.

steps.title: Universal and Palmer
steps.body:
**Universal (common in the USA):** permanent teeth 1–32 starting at the upper right third molar, running to the upper left (16), dropping to lower left third molar (17) and back to lower right (32). Primary teeth A–T.

**Palmer (Zsigmondy–Palmer):** a quadrant bracket with a number 1–8 (permanent) or letter A–E (primary). Upper right first molar = 6 in the upper-right bracket.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying FDI '21' is a lower tooth — it is the upper left central incisor.
- Forgetting that the patient's right is on the clinician's left on a chart.
- Mixing primary letters (Universal A–T) with Palmer letters (A–E per quadrant).

steps.title: Permanent eruption (approximate, years)
steps.body:
- First molars: 6–7
- Central incisors: 6–8 (lower usually before upper)
- Lateral incisors: 7–9
- First premolars: 10–12
- Canines: lower 9–10, upper 11–12
- Second premolars: 10–12
- Second molars: 11–13
- Third molars: 17–21 (variable)

Ranges vary between populations; use them as guides, not rules.

steps.title: Primary dentition
steps.body: Usually begins with lower central incisors around 6–10 months and is complete with second molars around 24–33 months. The first permanent molar erupts behind the last primary tooth and replaces nothing — parents often mistake it for a milk tooth.

steps.title: Clinical relevance
steps.body: Delayed eruption beyond the range, asymmetry over ~6 months between sides, or retained primary teeth with a clinically absent successor deserve a radiograph.

steps.title: Key identifying features
steps.body:
- **Maxillary first molar:** largest crown, oblique ridge, cusp of Carabelli often on mesiopalatal cusp, three roots (two buccal, one palatal).
- **Mandibular first molar:** five cusps (3 buccal, 2 lingual), two roots (mesial and distal).
- **Maxillary first premolar:** usually two roots (buccal and palatal), mesial crown concavity.
- **Mandibular second premolar:** two common forms — two-cusp (Y/H groove) or three-cusp (Y groove).
- **Maxillary canine:** longest root in the mouth.

steps.title: Side identification
steps.body: Find the crown's mesial surface (straighter, contact higher) and the root curvature (roots tend to curve distally). Then orient buccal/lingual.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling a maxillary second molar a first molar: the second molar is smaller, Carabelli trait is rare and roots are closer together.

steps.title: Differences
steps.body:
- Primary crowns are whiter, smaller, with pronounced cervical constriction and a cervical ridge.
- Enamel and dentine are thinner; pulp chambers relatively larger with prominent pulp horns (especially mesial) — caries reaches the pulp faster.
- Primary molar roots are thin, long and flared to make room for the developing premolar.
- Primary teeth hold space for successors, help speech and chewing.

steps.title: Why it matters clinically
steps.body: Large pulp horns explain why a 'small' cavity in a primary molar may already need pulp therapy, and why early loss without space maintenance can lead to crowding.

courses.title: Oral Histology & Tooth Development
courses.summary: Odontogenesis stages, enamel, dentine, pulp, cementum and periodontal ligament at histology-practical depth.
outcomes: Learners can sequence the stages of tooth development
Learners can describe enamel and dentine structure

scenes.text: A child has a congenitally missing lateral incisor.
The answer lies in tooth development.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Sequence
steps.body:
Initiation (dental lamina from oral ectoderm) → **bud** → **cap** (enamel organ, dental papilla, dental follicle) → **bell** (histodifferentiation & morphodifferentiation; inner/outer enamel epithelium, stellate reticulum, stratum intermedium) → apposition (enamel and dentine matrix) → maturation.

Enamel comes from ectoderm (ameloblasts); dentine and pulp from the dental papilla (ectomesenchyme, neural-crest derived); cementum, PDL and alveolar bone from the follicle.

steps.title: Hertwig's epithelial root sheath
steps.body: Fusion of inner and outer enamel epithelium below the crown; it maps root shape and induces root dentine. Remnants persist as **epithelial rests of Malassez** in the PDL — a source of radicular cysts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assigning enamel to mesoderm — enamel is the only ectodermal hard tissue of the tooth.

steps.title: Enamel
steps.body: About 96% mineral (hydroxyapatite) by weight, acellular, cannot regenerate. Structural unit: enamel rod (prism). Features: **striae of Retzius** (incremental lines), neonatal line, Hunter–Schreger bands, enamel tufts, lamellae, spindles.

steps.title: Dentine
steps.body:
About 70% mineral by weight. Odontoblast processes lie in tubules. Types: primary, secondary (formed after root completion, slowly throughout life), tertiary (reactionary or reparative, in response to stimuli). Incremental lines: von Ebner lines; contour lines of Owen.

**Hydrodynamic theory (Brännström):** fluid movement in open tubules stimulates pulpal nerves → sharp sensitivity.

steps.title: Clinical link
steps.body: Desensitising agents work by occluding tubules or by reducing nerve excitability (e.g. potassium salts).

steps.title: Pulp zones
steps.body: From periphery inward: odontoblastic layer → cell-free zone of Weil → cell-rich zone → pulp core (vessels and nerves). Pulp stones and diffuse calcification increase with age.

steps.title: Cementum and PDL
steps.body: Cementum: acellular (cervical, attachment) and cellular (apical, adaptive). PDL width roughly 0.15–0.38 mm. Principal fibre groups (alveolodental): **alveolar crest, horizontal, oblique (most numerous; resist vertical forces), apical, interradicular**; plus gingival fibres such as transseptal. Sharpey's fibres are embedded ends of collagen fibres in cementum and bone.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling transseptal fibres part of the alveolodental group — they run tooth-to-tooth over the crest and are counted with the gingival fibres.

scenes.text: A student sips sweet tea all day and develops multiple cavities.
Caries is a biofilm-mediated, sugar-driven disease.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Aetiology
steps.body: Keyes' triad (host/tooth, microflora, substrate) plus **time** (Newbrun). Acidogenic bacteria (mutans streptococci initiate; lactobacilli progress in dentine) ferment sugars → pH drops below the critical pH (~5.5 for enamel) → demineralisation. Frequency of sugar intake matters more than total amount.

steps.title: Zones of enamel caries (from deep to surface)
steps.body: **Translucent zone → dark zone → body of the lesion → surface zone.** The body has the greatest mineral loss; the surface zone appears relatively intact.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating every white-spot lesion with a drill — non-cavitated enamel lesions can remineralise with fluoride and diet control.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
**Inflammatory:** radicular (periapical) cyst — commonest odontogenic cyst, at apex of a non-vital tooth; residual cyst.

**Developmental:** dentigerous cyst — attached at the CEJ enclosing the crown of an unerupted tooth (commonly mandibular third molars, maxillary canines); **odontogenic keratocyst** — parakeratinised lining, high recurrence, posterior mandible, multiple in naevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome; lateral periodontal cyst; gingival cyst.

The 2017/2022 WHO classifications list odontogenic keratocyst as a cyst (it had been called keratocystic odontogenic tumour in 2005).

steps.title: Radiographic clue
steps.body: Pericoronal radiolucency attached at the CEJ → think dentigerous cyst; but ameloblastoma and OKC can look similar, so histopathology decides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Diagnosing a periapical radiolucency at a **vital** tooth as a radicular cyst — check vitality first.

scenes.text: A 52-year-old who chews tobacco with areca nut has a white patch on the buccal mucosa that does not rub off.
You must decide what to do.

steps.title: OPMDs
steps.body:
- **Leukoplakia:** white plaque of questionable risk, after excluding other known causes. Non-homogeneous (speckled, nodular, verrucous) has higher risk than homogeneous.
- **Erythroplakia:** red patch; highest malignant potential.
- **Oral submucous fibrosis:** strongly linked to areca nut; blanching, fibrous bands, reduced mouth opening.
- **Oral lichen planus:** reticular (Wickham striae) or erosive; chronic immune-mediated.

Risk factors: tobacco (smoked/smokeless), areca nut, alcohol, HPV for some oropharyngeal cancers.

steps.title: India context
steps.body: Smokeless tobacco and areca nut use make oral cancer one of the commonest cancers among men in India; early detection by visual examination saves lives.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Any red, white or ulcerated lesion that persists beyond about 2 weeks after removing a likely irritant needs specialist assessment and biopsy.

story.title: A swelling of the posterior mandible

scenes.text: A 30-year-old has painless expansion of the left posterior mandible.

steps.title: Differential diagnosis
steps.body: Multilocular radiolucency, posterior mandible, young adult: **ameloblastoma**, odontogenic keratocyst, central giant cell granuloma, odontogenic myxoma. Root resorption and buccolingual expansion favour ameloblastoma; OKC tends to grow along the bone with less expansion.

steps.title: Ameloblastoma
steps.body: Benign but locally aggressive epithelial odontogenic tumour. Common histological patterns: follicular and plexiform. Management is surgical, with margins; recurrence follows simple curettage.

steps.title: Order
steps.body: History → examination → imaging (OPG, CBCT) → incisional biopsy → definitive treatment planning.

scenes.text: A child with fever and many vesicles; a student with recurrent small ulcers; an adult with a single ulcer next to a broken tooth.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: Key ulcers
steps.body:
- **Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1):** usually children, fever, multiple vesicles → ulcers on gingiva and mucosa.
- **Recurrent herpes labialis:** vesicles on lip vermilion, prodromal tingling.
- **Recurrent aphthous stomatitis:** minor (<1 cm, heal in ~1–2 weeks without scarring), major (>1 cm, weeks, scarring), herpetiform (many tiny). Non-keratinised mucosa.
- **Traumatic ulcer:** source of trauma nearby; should heal within ~2 weeks of removing cause.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Ulcer >2–3 weeks, induration, rolled margins, fixation, lymph nodes, weight loss → urgent specialist referral.

steps.title: Location clue
steps.body: Recurrent intraoral HSV favours keratinised mucosa (hard palate, attached gingiva); aphthae favour non-keratinised mucosa.

steps.title: Forms
steps.body:
- **Pseudomembranous (thrush):** wipe-off white plaques.
- **Erythematous:** red, e.g. after antibiotics; denture stomatitis under upper dentures; median rhomboid glossitis.
- **Hyperplastic (candidal leukoplakia):** non-wipeable; biopsy needed.
- **Angular cheilitis:** fissures at the corners of the mouth (often Candida and/or S. aureus).

Predisposing factors: inhaled steroids, antibiotics, diabetes, dentures, xerostomia, immunosuppression (including HIV), extremes of age.

steps.title: Prevention for inhaler users
steps.body: Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each inhaled corticosteroid dose; a spacer also reduces deposition.

steps.title: Unexplained candidiasis
steps.body: Severe or recurrent candidiasis without an obvious cause should prompt a look for systemic factors such as diabetes or immunosuppression.

steps.title: Selected associations
steps.body:
- Iron/B12/folate deficiency: atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis, recurrent ulcers.
- Diabetes: periodontitis, xerostomia, candidiasis, delayed healing.
- HIV: oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV), candidiasis, Kaposi sarcoma, necrotising periodontal disease.
- Crohn's disease: cobblestone mucosa, linear ulcers, lip swelling.
- Leukaemia: gingival enlargement and bleeding.
- Drug-induced gingival overgrowth: phenytoin, ciclosporin, calcium-channel blockers (e.g. nifedipine, amlodipine).

steps.body: Recognise, document and refer to the physician — do not diagnose systemic disease alone.

steps.title: Note

steps.title: Healthy periodontium
steps.body: Gingiva (free and attached), PDL, cementum and alveolar bone. Healthy sulcus depth about 1–3 mm; biologic width (supracrestal tissue attachment) ≈ junctional epithelium + connective tissue attachment ≈ 2 mm.

steps.title: Pathogenesis
steps.body: Dysbiotic plaque biofilm → host inflammatory response. **Gingivitis**: inflammation without attachment loss, reversible. **Periodontitis**: loss of connective tissue attachment and bone, pocket formation; key pathogens include *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Tannerella forsythia*, *Treponema denticola* (the 'red complex'). Risk factors: smoking, diabetes, genetics, stress.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Equating pocket depth with disease severity — recession can hide attachment loss; use CAL.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
CAL = probing depth + recession (margin apical to CEJ).
If the margin is **coronal** to the CEJ (enlargement), CAL = PD − distance from CEJ to margin.

steps.title: Solved examples

1) PD 4 mm, recession 3 mm → CAL = **7 mm**.
2) PD 6 mm, gingival margin 2 mm coronal to CEJ → CAL = 6 − 2 = **4 mm**.

steps.title: Staging (severity & complexity)
steps.body:
- **Stage I:** interdental CAL 1–2 mm, radiographic bone loss <15% (coronal third).
- **Stage II:** CAL 3–4 mm, bone loss 15–33%.
- **Stage III:** CAL ≥5 mm, bone loss extending to mid-third of root and beyond; tooth loss due to periodontitis ≤4 teeth; complexity factors (PD ≥6 mm, vertical bone loss, furcation II–III).
- **Stage IV:** as III plus tooth loss ≥5 teeth or need for complex rehabilitation (masticatory dysfunction, bite collapse, <20 remaining teeth).

steps.title: Grading (rate of progression)
steps.body: Grade A slow, B moderate, C rapid — primary criterion %bone loss/age (<0.25, 0.25–1.0, >1.0). Modifiers: smoking (<10 cigarettes/day → B; ≥10 → C) and diabetes (HbA1c <7% → B; ≥7% → C).

steps.title: Procedures

steps.title: Angle's molar classification
steps.body:
- **Class I:** mesiobuccal cusp of upper first molar occludes in the buccal groove of the lower first molar.
- **Class II:** lower molar distal to Class I. Division 1 — proclined upper incisors, increased overjet. Division 2 — retroclined upper centrals, deep bite.
- **Class III:** lower molar mesial to Class I.

steps.title: British Standard incisor classification
steps.body: Class I: lower incisor edges occlude on or below the cingulum plateau of upper incisors. Class II/1: lower edges behind cingulum, upper incisors proclined/average, increased overjet. Class II/2: upper centrals retroclined, overjet usually minimal. Class III: lower edges anterior to cingulum plateau, reduced or reversed overjet.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Classifying on the canines alone or mixing skeletal and dental classes without saying which.

steps.title: Pressure–tension theory
steps.body: Light continuous force compresses the PDL on the **pressure side** → osteoclastic bone resorption; on the **tension side** PDL stretches → osteoblastic bone deposition. Excessive force → hyalinisation (cell-free zone), undermining resorption, delayed movement and root resorption risk.

steps.title: Types of movement
steps.body: Tipping (lowest force), bodily movement, rotation, extrusion (low force), intrusion (lowest, risk of root resorption), torque.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Assuming heavier force = faster movement; it often slows movement and harms roots.

statements.s: Bone resorbs on the pressure side.

steps.title: G.V. Black classes
steps.body:
- **Class I:** pits and fissures (occlusal of posterior teeth, buccal/lingual pits, palatal of maxillary incisors).
- **Class II:** proximal surfaces of premolars and molars.
- **Class III:** proximal of anterior teeth not involving the incisal angle.
- **Class IV:** proximal of anterior teeth involving the incisal angle.
- **Class V:** cervical third of facial/lingual surfaces.
- **Class VI (Simon):** incisal edges and cusp tips.

steps.title: ICDAS (summary)
steps.body: Visual codes 0–6: 0 sound; 1–2 visual enamel change (first after drying, then wet); 3 localised enamel breakdown; 4 underlying dark shadow from dentine; 5 distinct cavity with visible dentine; 6 extensive cavity. Codes 1–2 are usually managed non-operatively.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Classifying an MO cavity on a premolar as Class I because it includes the occlusal surface — any posterior proximal involvement makes it Class II.

steps.title: Material properties
steps.body:
- **Dental amalgam:** strong, durable, technique-tolerant, non-aesthetic, needs mechanical retention. Use is being phased down globally under the Minamata Convention on Mercury.
- **Resin composite:** aesthetic, bonds to enamel/dentine, conserves tooth; technique-sensitive (isolation essential), polymerisation shrinkage.
- **Glass-ionomer (GIC):** chemical adhesion, fluoride release, moisture-tolerant; lower strength — good for high-risk patients, cervical lesions, primary teeth, ART.
- **Resin-modified GIC:** better strength and light-cure command set.

steps.title: Decision rule
steps.body: Isolation possible + aesthetics → composite. Poor isolation or very high caries risk → GIC/RMGIC. Large load-bearing restorations → consider indirect onlay/crown.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Placing composite without adequate isolation — saliva contamination ruins the bond and causes early failure.

steps.title: Pulp diagnosis
steps.body: Short, sharp, provoked pain that stops on removing the stimulus → **reversible pulpitis**. Lingering pain or spontaneous pain → irreversible pulpitis. Vital tooth with deep caries and reversible pulpitis is a candidate for vital pulp therapy.

steps.title: Management
steps.body: Selective (partial) caries removal leaving firm/leathery dentine over the pulp, liner (e.g. calcium silicate/GIC as indicated), well-sealed restoration. steps.title: Kennedy classes
steps.body:
- **Class I:** bilateral edentulous areas posterior to remaining teeth.
- **Class II:** unilateral posterior edentulous area.
- **Class III:** unilateral edentulous area bounded by teeth both sides.
- **Class IV:** single bilateral anterior area crossing the midline (no modifications).

steps.title: Concentration rules
steps.body:
- A **2% solution = 20 mg/mL** (percent × 10).
- Adrenaline **1:80,000 = 12.5 µg/mL**; 1:100,000 = 10 µg/mL; 1:200,000 = 5 µg/mL.
- Dose = concentration × volume.

steps.body:
2 × 2.2 mL = 4.4 mL. Lidocaine = 4.4 × 20 = **88 mg**. Adrenaline = 4.4 × 12.5 = **55 µg**.

Always compare with the maximum recommended dose for the patient's weight given in your formulary/product information, and reduce for children, the elderly and medically compromised patients.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Aspirate before injecting; inject slowly. Signs of LA toxicity: circumoral tingling, slurred speech, tinnitus, drowsiness, twitching → stop, call for help, support airway, call 112.

steps.title: Direct (Halstead) technique
steps.body: Patient's mouth wide open. Palpate the coronoid notch with the thumb; needle from the contralateral premolars, about 1 cm above and parallel to the lower occlusal plane, lateral to the pterygomandibular raphe, advancing until bone contact (typically about 20–25 mm), withdraw slightly, aspirate, inject slowly ~1.5 mL. Lingual nerve is often anaesthetised as you withdraw; long buccal nerve needs a separate injection for buccal soft tissues of molars.

steps.title: Complications
steps.body: Positive aspiration (reposition), transient facial nerve palsy if injected into the parotid (posterior), trismus, haematoma, nerve injury (rare paraesthesia). If facial palsy: protect the eye, reassure, document.

steps.title: Failure
steps.body: Too low or too anterior placement; accessory innervation (mylohyoid). Alternatives: Gow-Gates, Vazirani–Akinosi, intraosseous/intraligamentary supplements; articaine buccal infiltration can help for lower first molars.

steps.title: IADT-style first aid
steps.body: Find the tooth, hold by the **crown** (not the root), rinse briefly in cold water or milk if dirty (no scrubbing), and **replant** immediately if possible; bite on a cloth. If not possible, store in milk, saline or the patient's saliva (not water) and come immediately.

steps.title: In the clinic
steps.body: Check the socket, replant/reposition, flexible splint for about 2 weeks, radiograph, tetanus status, consider antibiotics per guidelines, root canal treatment within ~2 weeks for teeth with closed apices, follow-up.

steps.title: Do not
steps.body: Do not replant a **primary** tooth — it may damage the developing permanent successor.

steps.title: Common emergencies
steps.body:
- **Vasovagal syncope** (commonest): lie flat, raise legs, loosen clothing, oxygen if trained; recovers quickly.
- **Hypoglycaemia** (diabetic, confused, sweaty): oral glucose if conscious; if unconscious — emergency care, glucagon per training.
- **Anaphylaxis**: urticaria, wheeze, hypotension, swelling — call 112, intramuscular adrenaline per your emergency protocol (anterolateral thigh), oxygen, lie flat (or sit if breathing difficulty).
- **Asthma attack**: patient's reliever inhaler (salbutamol), oxygen, escalate if no response.
- **Angina/MI**: GTN spray, aspirin per protocol, call 112.
- **Cardiac arrest**: CPR 30:2, AED.

steps.title: ABCDE
steps.body: Assess Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure. Call for help early. Every dental clinic should have an emergency kit, oxygen and an AED, and staff trained in BLS.

steps.body: Document times, observations and drugs given.

steps.title: Fluoride toothpaste
steps.body: Use a fluoride toothpaste (at least 1000 ppm F) from the first tooth: **smear/rice-grain** amount under 3 years; **pea-sized** from 3–6 years; supervise brushing twice daily; spit, don't rinse.

scenes.text: A 6-year-old has a deep carious lesion on 84; carious exposure with bleeding that stops easily.
Pulpotomy or pulpectomy?

steps.title: Choosing
steps.body:
- **Indirect pulp therapy:** deep caries, no exposure, no irreversible symptoms.
- **Pulpotomy:** carious exposure, coronal pulp inflamed but radicular pulp vital (haemorrhage controlled within a few minutes). Medicaments: MTA/calcium silicate, ferric sulphate, (formocresol historically).
- **Pulpectomy:** irreversible pulpitis or necrosis with resorbable filling (zinc oxide–eugenol, iodoform-based pastes).
- **Extraction:** pathological root resorption >1/3, furcation lesion extensive, unrestorable, near exfoliation.

steps.title: Restore
steps.body: Preformed metal crown after pulp therapy gives the best long-term seal on primary molars.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using non-resorbable gutta-percha in primary teeth — it interferes with exfoliation.

scenes.text: You examine a 12-year-old: 3 decayed, 1 missing due to caries, 2 filled permanent teeth.

steps.title: Note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training or a professional licence.

steps.title: DMFT/dmft
steps.body: D = decayed, M = missing due to caries, F = filled — counted per **tooth** (T) or per **surface** (S, DMFS). Capitals = permanent; lowercase dmft = primary. A tooth counts once (decayed and filled → D). Teeth missing for orthodontic/other reasons are not counted as M. WHO index age: 12 years for global comparison.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: D 3 + M 1 + F 2 = **DMFT 6**. Group mean = sum of DMFT ÷ number examined. Ten children with total DMFT 18 → mean **1.8**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Counting an orthodontically extracted premolar as M; counting a decayed-and-filled tooth twice.

scenes.text: In a village survey of 400 adults, 120 have periodontitis.
Compute prevalence; then a one-year incidence.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Prevalence** = existing cases ÷ population at a point in time. **Incidence (risk)** = new cases during a period ÷ population at risk at start. Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration (in steady state).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1) 120/400 = **30%** prevalence.
2) Of 280 disease-free adults, 14 develop periodontitis in a year → incidence = 14/280 = **5% per year**.

steps.title: Study designs
steps.body: Cross-sectional → prevalence; cohort → incidence and relative risk; case–control → odds ratio; RCT → efficacy of interventions.

scenes.text: In a village, many children have brown mottled teeth; the water source is a borewell.
Investigate and advise.

steps.title: Fluoride levels
steps.body: WHO guideline for fluoride in drinking water: **1.5 mg/L**. India's drinking water standard (IS 10500) sets an acceptable limit of 1.0 mg/L and a permissible limit of 1.5 mg/L in the absence of an alternative source. Endemic fluorosis occurs in several Indian states with high-fluoride groundwater. Higher long-term intake can cause skeletal fluorosis.

steps.title: Actions
steps.body: Test water; provide safe alternative sources or defluoridation (e.g. activated alumina, Nalgonda technique); nutrition (calcium, vitamin C); continue age-appropriate fluoride toothpaste — topical benefits remain while swallowing is minimised; refer suspected skeletal fluorosis.

steps.title: Indices
steps.body: Dean's fluorosis index grades normal → questionable → very mild → mild → moderate → severe.
